title: Oneva (Disrupt SF 2017 final)

transcript.text: 43% of professional women with children leave the workforce. 43%. That's a huge number, and I know because I'm one of them. I quit my job as a CFO at Seagate because I had a child, we had a home, and a husband. Too many of us are forced to choose between work and family every single day. When I chose to become one of those 40% who did return to the workforce, you can imagine my frustration when I was unable to find trusted care anywhere in the marketplace.

And that's when Oneva was born. The Oneva Construe care platform allows our users to conveniently view, book, approve, and pay for FBI background care givers. We are currently in the market with Microsoft employees delivering house cleaning, elder care, infant care, pet care, driving, and other services that busy professionals all need as a wellness benefit. Rather than tell you how convenient and easy it is to use the Oneva platform, let's cut to a demo so you can see for yourselves.

Please, let's start the demo. So my husband of 31 years, Bob Gardine, 10 patents, three exits. We've been married 31 years, and we still have a minor child at home. Can you believe that? We've been working really hard to prepare for Disrupt, and we deserve a night out. We live in Oakland, and we love Scots out on the water. But we need care for our daughter. So let's go ahead and see what caregivers are available to come and provide care for our child.

And because we're so excited about this event, we're going to call it our celebratory night out. As you can see, our algorithm has matched a number of caregivers who meet our needs. Let's take a look at Belaine and see what she has to say. My name is Belaine, and I would love to be your caregiver. I care for children and elders, and I offer driving services to help my families get to school and appointments.

I love meeting new people, and I get great satisfaction, helping them however I can. Awesome. Now that we've heard from Belaine, let's see your credentials. With a simple click, I can see that FBI background check, that first aid certification and that degree from San Francisco State. Let's go and book her for this evening. Let's go ahead and cut back to the PowerPoint. As we design this platform, we realize that we could impact more families and more markets by designing for the enterprise.

And that's when Microsoft joined our team. Fred Till, General Manager Benefits at Microsoft, came to me and he said, I need the Oneva Konshir's care platform so that I can win in the talent wars. He said he needed one more innovative arrow in his quiver so he could go out and attract and retain the best and the brightest. And that's exactly what we do today. Moreover, we're able to attract and retain the best workers because we focus on worker safety, a job career, and living wages.

Yes, we know there are others in the market today providing care direct to consumer, and we know those marketplaces are filled with landmines for many, including their investors. You're wondering how we monetize this relationship with Microsoft. Well, here's what we do today. We simply mark up the cost of the caregiver, and that's how we make our money. Today in the San Francisco Bay Area, Microsoft employees are able to pay for these services using their credit card, their debit card, payroll reduction, and also employer provided stipend.

But we can produce that FSA reimbursement receipt needed so that Microsoft employees can get those pre-tax dollars back that they spent in our platform. Yes, we're attacking multiple multi-billion dollar markets, and I'm humbled to say that this certified minority-owned provider is the only player in this market and in this time. Microsoft absolutely is our first pilot, and we're excited to say that we have others who are anxious to join our team, including Oracle.

I'm Anita of Oneva. I solve real problems like elder care and extending women's careers. Oniva means trust and we care for yours like they're ours. Thank you. Judges. Can you talk a little bit about how long you've been working with Microsoft, how often employees use it, what the frequency looks like, and if there's a stack ranking of the services that they use most to least? Absolutely. We began our relationship with Microsoft in December 2014.

That's when I was approached by Fred Till, and we began that collaborative process. They've worked with us extensively while we operated in market in the consumer space, operating providing infant to elder and care and other services. When we launched our pilot here in the San Francisco Bay Area in February, to our surprise, the average user was male, 65% of the time, and requested on average 2.2 different services.

brief.headline: Dig deeper: the Microsoft pilot is real, but it is only a pilot, the 'only player' claim is contradicted by the founder's own words, and the company appears to no longer be operating.
brief.summary: Oneva sells a platform for booking FBI-background-checked caregivers (child, elder, pet, cleaning, driving) as an employer-sponsored wellness benefit, and makes money by marking up caregiver cost. The Microsoft pilot held up: press reports a February 2017 pilot giving about 3,000 Bay Area employees access. The live framing drifted, though. 'In the market with Microsoft' became 'our first pilot', and 'no trusted care anywhere' plus 'only player' became an admission that direct-to-consumer competitors exist. Revenue, pilot traction (2.2 services per user, 65% male), the Oracle interest and the founder and husband credentials are all unverified. Our web check also found that Oneva appears to be no longer operating.
strengths: Pilot with Microsoft is corroborated by TechCrunch and the Kiva business center: roughly 3,000 Bay Area employees given access starting February 2017.
Clear enterprise-benefit wedge, with a named Microsoft benefits sponsor and payment options including payroll deduction, employer stipend and FSA receipts.
Simple markup monetization and early usage data (2.2 services per user, 40% requesting three services) suggest breadth of demand, if verified.
Large addressable categories: child care and home care are each sized at tens of billions of dollars or more by independent analysts.

red_flags.text: Company appears to be no longer operating per our web check, which undermines everything resting on the pilot and the enterprise thesis. Status and reason for wind-down are unexplained.

Microsoft traction is narrower than first framed. The opening said 'in the market with Microsoft employees', but later it was 'our first pilot'. There is no evidence of a signed paid contract or conversion beyond the pilot, and only access (about 3,000 employees) is documented, not usage.

'Only player in this market' and 'no trusted care anywhere' are contradicted by the founder's own admission that direct-to-consumer care marketplaces exist. The enterprise-channel differentiation was not demonstrated.

Unit economics and traction are unverified: markup percentage, who pays it, revenue and margin per booking are not disclosed. Whether all listed services (infant, elder, pet, driving) were actually fulfilled in the pilot is unknown, as are the booking counts behind the 2.2 services per user.

Pipeline claim rests on 'anxious to join, including Oracle' with no LOI or pilot. Founder and husband credentials (Seagate CFO, 10 patents, three exits) are unverified. The headline 43% statistic is about 20 years old and overstates 'leave the workforce'.

questions: What is Oneva's current operating status, and if it stopped operating, why? Did the Microsoft pilot convert to a paid contract?
How many of the roughly 3,000 eligible Microsoft employees registered, booked at least once, and rebooked, and which services were actually fulfilled?
What is the markup percentage, who pays it, and what were revenue and gross margin per booking after background checks and support?
Which direct-to-consumer and enterprise care-benefit competitors do you face, and why does the enterprise channel give you a durable advantage?
Is there any signed LOI or active pilot with Oracle or others, and who is the economic buyer and expected sales cycle?

Pilot funnel data by month (eligible, registered, booked, repeat users) and a booking ledger by service category showing requested versus fulfilled
Pilot P&L with per-booking revenue, caregiver cost, markup and pricing sheet
Pipeline list with stage and contact roles, and any emails or LOIs from Oracle and others

live_notes: Opening said 'currently in the market with Microsoft employees'; later called Microsoft 'our first pilot', a narrower scope.
Opened with no trusted care anywhere in the marketplace and 'only player', then conceded others provide care direct to consumer.
In Q&A, said the Microsoft relationship began December 2014 and that Oneva ran a consumer business before the February pilot. This was not in the pitch and sits oddly with 'only player'.
New live-only data: pilot users were male 65% of the time, requested 2.2 services on average, and 40% requested three. The answer was cut off before the ranking of services.
Oracle was named as interested only in the closing, with no detail on stage.

outcome: Finalist (runner-up), did not win TechCrunch Disrupt SF 2017 Startup Battlefield
